notes:
I've put together notes for all 18 verses, but some verses have much less material than others. I ran out of search and page-fetch calls before I could read the verse-by-verse Gill, Ellicott and Pulpit Commentary pages for vv. 10–18. Several things I looked for don't appear here because I didn't find them: Wesleyan, Lutheran, Pentecostal (ag.org) and Orthodox sources, NET Bible notes on this chapter, and any prosperity teacher in their own words.

## God's commission to Joshua (vv. 1–9)

**v. 1**
- **Moses is gone, but God's work continues.** Guzik notes that Moses would never lead the people into the land, however great he was. He quotes Maclaren: Joshua – who was not a young man at this time – had spent his entire career previously as the assistant of Moses. Joshua found that now it was his time to lead, but only after God had prepared him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/
- **The Spirit in Joshua.** Guzik says Joshua's most important qualification was being a "man in whom is the Spirit" (Numbers 27:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/
- **Two words for "servant."** Precept Austin points out that Moses is called *'ebed* ("servant") and Joshua *sharath* ("assistant"). Joshua learned to lead by serving under Moses, and at the end of the book (24:29) he too is called "servant of the LORD." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **Joshua's name.** Guzik says the name Joshua translates as "Jesus" in the Greek language of New Testament times. Joshua is an enduring picture or type of Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/

**v. 2**
- **"Moses is dead" is a call to act.** George Bush (19th century) says Joshua already knew Moses had died. The words really mean the people are without a leader and head to conduct them into the promised land, and "his place should be immediately filled." https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **"Workmen die, but God lives."** Theodore Epp, quoted on Precept Austin, makes this point. The work of God is in no way hindered by the death of His servants, no matter how eminent they may be. The workman may be removed, but the work goes forward. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60741/
- **The whole people are called.** Precept Austin notes that the command goes to "all this people," not only to Joshua. God is repeating His promises to the patriarchs. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **vv. 2–4 as a map of the book.** Guzik sees an outline here: crossing the Jordan, conquering Canaan, then dividing the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/

**v. 3**
- **Given, but it must be claimed.** Guzik says the whole land was given, but they could only possess that which they claimed... What they took must be fought for against determined opposition. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-1.cfm
- **Unconditional or conditional?** J. Vernon McGee says the land was given to Israel. Israel's ownership was unconditional. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62593/ Precept Austin's own comment adds a qualification. The gift was unconditional because Israel could not earn it, but in another sense it was "conditioned" on obedience. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **Echo of Deuteronomy.** Madvig, quoted by Guzik, notes that vv. 3–5a closely follow the wording of Deuteronomy 11:24–25a. He takes this as evidence the author meant Joshua's work to be the fulfilment of the Pentateuch. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/

**v. 4**
- **The borders.** Bush describes them as running south to north from the wilderness to Lebanon, and east to west from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **A real land.** Guzik says the precise borders show this was a physical land, not a "spiritual" one. Quoting Madvig, he says the promise was not fully met until David and Solomon. "The land of the Hittites" was a name Egypt and Babylon used for Palestine even after the Hittites had left. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/

**v. 5**
- **God's presence is the guarantee.** Guzik writes that victory is assured not because Joshua is a great leader, or because Israel is a great nation, but because God is a great God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **Applied to all believers.** Guzik notes that "I will not leave you nor forsake you" repeats Deuteronomy 31:6 and is quoted in Hebrews 13:5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/

**vv. 6–7**
- **The repeated command.** Brian Bill notes that God says "be strong and courageous" three times. He says the word "strong" comes from twisting ropes together and "courageous" means to persist and conquer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-joshua-brian-bill
- **Confidence in God, not self.** Guzik: This bold courage would not be in Joshua himself, but in God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-1.cfm
- **Courage to obey.** Bush says the Hebrew word "only" (*rak*) in v. 7 signals that a condition is being set. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62593/ Donald Campbell says Joshua's victories are explained by his living by the Law of Moses, the only Scripture written at the time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary

**v. 8**
- **Word on the lips, in the mind, in practice.** Guzik says Scripture had to be on his lips..., in his mind..., and he had to do it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-1.cfm
- **Calvin.** Calvin says the command is to keep studying all life long, because errors creep in whenever study stops. Anything attempted in contempt of God's word ends in failure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/1-8.html
- **Geneva Bible note.** It is not possible to govern well, without the continual study of God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/1-8.htm
- **Clarke.** A copy of the law kept in the sanctuary was not enough; Joshua needed his own copy and had to consult it constantly. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/joshua/1-8.html
- **Gill.** He applies the promised success to Joshua's wars with the Canaanites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/1-8.html
- **"Act wisely."** Keil & Delitzsch read the last phrase as "act wisely" (compare Deuteronomy 29:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/1-8.html Precept Austin adds that the two Hebrew verbs differ. The one translated "success" (*sakal*) basically means to act with insight or prudence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua_18_commentary
- **Echo in Psalm 1.** Ellicott notes that Psalm 1:2–3 takes up this verse. https://biblehub.com/joshua/1-8.htm

**v. 9**
- **God's presence matters more than Joshua's effort.** Guzik says Joshua's success did not depend solely on his ability to keep God's word. It depended even more on God's presence with him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-1.cfm
- **"Have I not commanded you?"** Precept Austin notes the NET rendering, "Don't be afraid and don't panic." Joshua was human and needed reassurance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62593/

## Joshua prepares the people (vv. 10–18)

**vv. 10–11**
- **"Then."** Precept Austin notes that Joshua acts only after receiving God's word of encouragement. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **Preparing provisions.** Brian Bill says the people had to get over the "manna mindset" and start planning. Trusting God and planning go together. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-joshua-brian-bill
- **The three days.** Guzik applies them to believers: days of waiting are always days of preparation in God's work. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary

**vv. 12–15**
- **Background in Numbers 32.** Utley explains that these tribes wanted land east of the Jordan for its pasture. Moses required them to fight alongside their brothers first, and even to go into battle ahead of them. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20217 Dale Ralph Davis says these verses gain theological weight when read alongside Numbers 32. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **Helping the body.** Guzik applies v. 14 to the church: We should never refuse to help a brother in need because our own state is settled. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- **A dissenting note.** Epp sees "a rather sad note" in vv. 10–18. The eastern tribes did not all have the same degree of separation from the evil around them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60741/

**vv. 16–18**
- **National unity.** Guzik says the tribes overcame the temptation to see the eastern tribes as separate from the rest of Israel. Their acceptance of Joshua confirmed what God had said earlier in the chapter. https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide2017-jos/jos-1.cfm
- **"Only be strong and courageous" (v. 18).** The people repeat God's own words to Joshua, which Guzik reads as God confirming His word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-1.cfm Brian Bill says the people promise to follow his leadership and then they tell him to not be afraid. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-joshua-brian-bill

## Where Christian readings differ

I didn't find sources that set out formal denominational disagreements on this chapter. The main differences among teachers are these.

**vv. 1–2: Moses as a picture of the law (typology)**
- Spurgeon: Moses could not conduct the people into the promised land. Nor can the law bring any man to heaven. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/encourage-your-minister
- Chuck Smith says the law can bring you to the border but cannot take you in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/joshua-1.html
- Guzik extends the picture: Moses stood for the law, Miriam for the prophets and Aaron for the priesthood, and only Joshua ("Jesus") leads in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/
- McGee adds a different reason. Moses could not lead Israel into the land because of his failure. The problem was not with the Law but with Moses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- Precept Austin warns readers to be a Berean about F. B. Meyer's frequent use of typology. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-resources

**Is Canaan a picture of heaven?**
- Precept Austin says many hymns treat the Jordan as death and Canaan as heaven. It calls this Biblically inaccurate, because once Joshua led the Israelites across the Jordan, they immediately experienced warfare. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/joshua-1-commentary
- Guzik, citing Hebrews 4 and Spurgeon, reads Canaan as the believer's present rest, not heaven. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-1/
- John Lloyd's older commentary does treat the journey as a picture of entering heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/Joshua_commentaries

## Other views

**Catholic**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the Church Fathers often called the book "Jesus Nave." To the Fathers Josue is an historical person and a type of the Messias. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/joshua

**Modern scholarship**
- The Biblical Illustrator reports the critical view that assigns chapter 1 to the "Deuteronomist." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/joshua.html
- Bible.org's bibliography lists commentaries (Soggin, Hamlin) that treat the book as a "Deuteronomistic" composition. https://bible.org/article/selected-bibliography-joshua
- A Bible Odyssey scholar says the Joshua conquest account seems to contradict Judges in some respects and parts of the archaeological record, Jericho in particular. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/video-gallery/archaeology-and-conquest/

**Prosperity teaching (v. 8)**
I only found critics' descriptions of this reading:
- Precept Austin says the verse is NOT a promise of material or financial success. The context is military success, and there is no mention of finances in the entire first chapter of Joshua. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua_18_commentary
- A Bible Hub article calls prosperity here a corporate covenant outcome, not an isolated personal windfall. https://biblehub.com/q/Joshua_1_8_and_biblical_prosperity.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes take a middle position: prosperity may include material blessing, but always includes fruitfulness, peace, and steadfast witness. https://biblehub.com/joshua/1-8.htm
- Chuck Smith speaks more broadly. To people seeking success he says these are the rules to prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/1-8.html
